name: Per-kernel launch and dispatch overhead at batch 1
arithmetic_intensity: Not a byte/flop quantity - it is a fixed CPU-side cost per kernel launch, measured in microseconds, paid before any bytes move. At batch 1 a decode step runs on the order of a few hundred to a few thousand kernels (attention, norms, activations, GEMMs, residuals, sampling), so launch and dispatch overhead can be a visible fraction of step latency even when the GPU work itself is only tens of microseconds. This is why CUDA Graphs exist: capture the launch sequence once, replay it, and remove per-kernel launch overhead - the mechanism engines reach for precisely when B is 1 and every op is too small to amortize its own dispatch. The consequence for scheduling is that CUDAGraph requires static shapes, which is why FlashInfer's load-balanced scheduler is designed to stay compatible with CUDAGraph's static configuration.
scales_with: batch_size (inverse - at high batch each launch amortizes over more work and this stops mattering)
num_kernels_per_layer (model depth x ops per layer)
host CPU speed and driver overhead (this is a CPU-bound cost)
static-vs-dynamic shapes (dynamic shapes force re-capture or eager launch)
workarounds: CUDA Graphs (and equivalents): capture and replay the launch sequence to eliminate per-kernel launch overhead (NVIDIA Technical Blog, Alan Gray, 2019)
Kernel fusion - fewer, bigger kernels amortize launch overhead across more work
Persistent / megakernel designs where one launch covers a whole layer or the whole step
Static shape discipline so graphs stay valid and capturable
Batching, which raises the work per launch without touching the launch count
notes: Design consequence: at batch 1 the fastest kernel is often the one that is launched, not the one with the best FLOPs or bandwidth utilization, so launch overhead sets a floor on inter-token latency that no amount of FLOPS improvement can move. Two practical rules follow. For engine authors: if a decode loop is CPU-launch-bound, raising batch or capturing graphs will beat optimizing any single kernel. For hardware designers: the cost is CPU-side and driver-mediated, so fast host memory, low-latency launch paths and driver maturity matter for small-batch latency in a way they do not for throughput - and it means a part with strong FLOPS but a weak host interface can lose the batch-1 latency race outright. Note this class overlaps with norm_softmax and sampling: fusing those is simultaneously an HBM saving and a launch saving, which is why fusion is the first thing any decode path tries.
